title: Repent a day before you die (Avot 2:10)
word: Repent a day before you die
hook: Rabbi Eliezer: repent one day before your death, and no one knows the day, so every day

segments.voice: Yesterday, five students, five answers, and the one that held all the others. Your line was a good heart. What did a good heart choose? Today, one of those students speaks. Day two hundred fifty-eight.

Rabbi Eliezer's students heard him say something that sounded impossible: repent one day before your death. So they asked the obvious question. How is anyone supposed to know which day that is? Eliezer was one of the five students from yesterday, the one his own teacher compared to a plastered cistern that never loses a drop. He had heard a great deal and lost none of it. And his answer takes a far-off day and sets it down right here, in this one.
screen: `AN IMPOSSIBLE INSTRUCTION.` → `WHICH DAY IS THAT?` → `A CISTERN THAT LOSES NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Eliezer said three things. Let your friend's honor be as dear to you as your own. Don't be quick to anger. And repent one day before your death. That last one is the riddle, and the Talmud records his answer to the students who asked about it. Does anyone know the day he'll die? All the more reason to repent today, in case you die tomorrow. Then all your days will be spent in repentance. The word is teshuvah. It's usually translated repentance, but it really means return, or turning. You notice you've wandered off the path, and you turn back toward it. No groveling required, no drama. Just a turn. The Talmud then tells a parable. A king invited his servants to a banquet, but didn't say when. The wise ones dressed in their best and waited by the palace door. After all, a palace is never short of anything; the feast could start any minute. The foolish ones went off to their work, saying, there's no banquet without a lot of preparation first. Suddenly the king called them in. The wise walked in dressed and ready. The foolish came in dirty from work, and weren't allowed to sit at the table. The verse that goes with it is in Ecclesiastes, which in the JPS translation reads, "Let thy garments be always white." Not out of fear. Just ready. Rabbi Eliezer's advice isn't a threat. It's a schedule. If today might be the day, then today is the day to turn.
screen: `THREE PIECES OF ADVICE.` · `NOBODY KNOWS THE DAY.` · `TESHUVAH: TURNING BACK.` · `THE KING'S BANQUET.` · then, large: `LET THY GARMENTS BE ALWAYS WHITE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a small turn, today. Settle, and breathe. Look back over the day so far, slowly, from waking up until now. Notice one moment where you drifted from the person you mean to be. A sharp word. A shortcut. A kindness skipped. Don't argue with it, and don't punish yourself. Just name it. Then picture the turn back: what would one small step in the right direction look like, before tonight? If you pray, you can bring it to God. The bell holds the time.
Repent a day before you die. Rabbi Eliezer's riddle: nobody knows the day, so turn back today, and every day is a day of teshuvah.
screen: `REPENT A DAY BEFORE YOU DIE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: repent today. Find one turn you've been saving for someday, a sorry, a habit, a call, and make the first small move before you sleep. Day two hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Jewish tradition treats teshuvah, returning, as possible every day, not only on Yom Kippur, and the traditional bedtime prayers include a moment of forgiving others before sleep.

notes: Avot is paraphrased (outline follows Taylor 1897). Numbering: 2:10 common, 2:15 in some editions.
Ecclesiastes 9:8 is quoted from the KJV; JPS 1917 is believed to read the same for this clause but was not verified.

Shabbat 153a: the students' question, Eliezer's answer, and the parable of the king's banquet (told there in the name of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai); the script does not name the parable's teller; confirm.
'A cistern that never lost a drop' is Yochanan ben Zakkai's praise of Eliezer in Avot 2:8.

Editor review: Ecclesiastes 9:8 now cited from JPS 1917 (same clause), not the KJV. The hook and practice repeated day 244's angle (the put-off list, the call, the apology, the first small step); the hook now drops into the students' question, and the practice is a look back over the day for one place to turn. The verse is no longer credited to 'the rabbis' (in Shabbat 153a Eliezer himself cites it). howItsDone 'many Jews' replaced by the bedtime-prayer forgiveness line.
